In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
branching in 1 does reduce flexibility at the (1 → 3)-linkage but does not affect flexibility at the ( 1 → 4) linkage.
the glycosidic bond between ManNAc and Glc in 1 is more flexible than the glycosidically linked Glc and the Rha residue in the trisaccharides.
the flexibility of the (1→4) linkage is not significantly influenced by branching at the reducing end.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the (1→4) linkage in 2 is flexible enough to adopt all orientations of the glycosidic torsion angles, whereas the (1→ 3) linkage in both 1 and 3 is restricted to the S2 region.
the flexibility of glycosidically linked saccharide units is an important parameter which has to be considered when interpreting NMR data of oligo- and polysaccharides.
the glycosidic bond in the (1→4)-linked β-ManNAc-(l)-Rha 2 is flexible and that the (1→2)-linked α-Glc-(l)-Rho 3 is rigid.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the flexibility of glycosidically linked carbohydrates cannot be neglected when studying the structure of oligosaccharides or polysaccharides, and that the flexibility is not only a function of the glycosidic bond itself but also of the overall oligosaccharide or polysaccharide structure.

the flexibility of a branched trisacharide is reduced compared to the constituent di- and trisaccharides, and that the (1→4) linkage of the branched trisacheride is less flexible than the (1→ 4) linkage of a disaccharide.
flexibility of glycosidically linked oligosaccharides should not be neglected in the analysis of NOE-derived conformational data.
